transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, it wasn't really my idea. They sent me from occupational health. They're saying my weight is dangerously low for someone running presses and doing fabrication all day... but I honestly thought I was just getting leaner and more disciplined. 

You really have to be disciplined in the shop, especially right now. We just got this new hydraulic press last week, and it's a total beast. I've been trying to tell my supervisor, Dave—he's been there for like twenty years, always wears these ridiculous neon suspenders, it's so distracting—that the safety guard on the new press is sticking. I took a few engineering classes back in college, so I know a little bit about how the calibration is supposed to work. But Dave just brushes it off. He's more worried about me than the actual equipment, apparently. So anyway, yeah, they made me come here, but I really need to get back soon because if Dave tries to fix that guard himself, he's going to shut down the whole line.
Can you tell me more about your eating habits lately? Have you been intentionally losing weight, and if so, how have you been doing it?

I mean, I guess it's intentional, but I just look at it as being disciplined. Most days I just stick to coffee before the early shift. You have to get there so early anyway, and honestly, the breakroom coffee is terrible. Dave buys this cheap bulk stuff that tastes like literal battery acid. I told him we should all just chip in for a decent pod machine, but he says it's a fire hazard. A fire hazard! In a fabrication shop where we literally have sparks flying all day. It makes absolutely no sense. 

But anyway, yeah, at lunch I'll usually just have maybe half a protein bar. And then a small bowl of vegetables after my evening yoga class. Yoga has been a total lifesaver for my back, actually. Standing on concrete for ten hours a day really compresses your lumbar spine, and my instructor, Chloe—she's this former ballet dancer, super intense but really great—she showed me these specific stretches for sciatica. I really should show Dave those stretches, his posture is terrible when he's leaning over the drafting table. 

But yeah, the coffee, the half a bar, and the vegetables, that's pretty much it. If I eat more than that, the whole day just feels completely out of control. Like I'm losing my grip on everything, you know? I just need things to be orderly. Which is exactly why that safety guard on the press is bothering me so much.

Can you tell me more about why eating more than your usual makes you feel like you're losing control? Has that fear of feeling 'out of control' ever led you to restrict your eating even when you knew you needed more food?

It's just... if I step on the scale in the morning and it goes up even a little bit, I just absolutely panic. It's like I'm going to lose all the control I've worked so hard for and end up heavy again, you know? So, yeah, even if I know I probably need a little more food because I'm doing a heavy fabrication shift, I just restrict it anyway. I can't risk it. I have to keep the numbers exactly where they belong. 

Speaking of scales, actually, we have this massive industrial freight scale at the loading dock for the pallets, and it is supposed to be calibrated every single month. But you know Dave. He totally skipped the November maintenance. I was trying to weigh a pallet of aluminum extrusion the other day—we use the 6061 grade mostly, it's way better for machining and welding than the 6063, though I guess it really depends on the tensile strength the client wants for their specific project. Anyway, the freight scale was reading at least forty pounds light! 

I told Dave, if we ship this out to the aerospace contractor with the wrong manifest weight, they are going to reject the entire lot. And do you think he listened? No. He just stood there chewing on his cinnamon toothpick. He always has one of those in his mouth. I'm pretty sure that's terrible for your enamel. My dentist, Dr. Aris, told me years ago that chewing on wood splinters causes these tiny micro-abrasions on your gums, and eventually you get receding gumlines. I should probably warn Dave about that, actually, before his teeth just fall out right on the shop floor. That would be a massive biohazard.
After eating, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or exercise excessively to control your weight or shape?

No, I don't do any of that throwing up stuff or taking pills. I just stick to my routine and the yoga, you know? Though, speaking of routines, I was trying to explain to Chloe—my yoga instructor—about the repetitive motion stress from running the TIG welder. You have to hold the torch at this very specific angle, and after a few hours, your wrist just locks up. 

I actually tried to get Dave to order these ergonomic torch handles. I found them in this catalog from a supplier in Germany. They use this specialized heat-resistant polymer that absorbs the micro-vibrations from the arc. But Dave just laughed and said back in his day they just wrapped electrical tape around the handle until it was thick enough to grip. Electrical tape! Can you imagine? The adhesive gets all gummy when it heats up, and then you've got this sticky black residue all over your gloves. 

And good luck getting that off the leather. I have these really nice deerskin TIG gloves, they're so soft, you can actually feel the filler rod feeding through your fingers. They cost me like fifty bucks, but they're totally worth it for the precision. I'm not ruining them with Dave's cheap electrical tape. So I just do the wrist stretches Chloe showed me. But yeah, no throwing up or anything like that. Just the stretches.
Do you feel like your weight or body shape is significantly different from what others might see, even if they tell you that you look healthy or underweight?

I mean, people at the shop tell me I look fine, or even that I'm getting too thin, but they just don't see what I see. When I catch my reflection in the shop window, or even just in the bathroom mirror, all I can focus on is my stomach and my thighs. They just look so big to me, and it honestly just ruins how I feel about myself for the rest of the entire day. 

And speaking of the bathroom mirror, the lighting in the employee restroom is absolutely atrocious. Dave installed these cheap fluorescent tubes that buzz constantly. It's like a low-grade hum that just drills into your skull. And they flicker! It's like being in a horror movie. I told him we should switch to LED panels. They're so much more energy-efficient, and you can get them in a daylight color temperature, which is way better for your circadian rhythm. 

I actually read this fascinating article about circadian rhythms and shift work. It said that exposure to cool-toned light during the day can boost your alertness by like, thirty percent. But Dave just grumbled something about the overhead budget. The overhead budget! Meanwhile, he just bought a brand new F-250 for himself. It's got the extended cab and the towing package, which is totally unnecessary because we use the freight company for all our large deliveries. He just wanted it because it looks tough. But yeah, I just... I see myself in that awful lighting, and I just look so heavy, no matter what anyone else says.

Can you describe how you feel when you think about gaining even a small amount of weight, and does that feeling seem in line with how much weight you've actually lost or where you currently are in terms of your body weight?

I mean, I think I already mentioned this, but if the scale goes up even a little bit, I just absolutely panic. It's like this overwhelming dread that I'm going to lose all the control I've worked so incredibly hard for, and I'll just end up heavy again. It doesn't matter what I actually weigh right now or how much I've lost, the fear is just always there, you know? 

And speaking of losing things, I was looking for my favorite tungsten electrodes the other day. I swear, they just vanished into thin air. I use the 2% lanthanated ones—they have the blue band on them. They're the best because they hold a really sharp point for a long time, and you don't get as much spit-out when you're welding on AC. 

Anyway, I was tearing my workstation apart looking for them, and I found this old stash of polishing compound that I thought we ran out of like six months ago. It was the green rouge, which is perfect for getting that mirror finish on stainless steel. I was actually going to use it on this custom exhaust manifold I was working on for a client. They wanted it to look show-quality, which is a huge pain because you have to go through like five different grits of sandpaper before you even touch the buffing wheel. 

If you skip a grit, you just end up highlighting the scratches instead of removing them. It's a whole process. You have to be so meticulous, kind of like how I have to be with my food and the scale. If I'm not completely on top of it, everything just falls apart.
Would you say that your weight or the way you look determines how you feel about yourself overall?

Yeah, I mean, it pretty much controls everything. I think I said before, like, if I catch my reflection in the shop window, or even just in that awful bathroom mirror we have, all I can see is my stomach and my thighs. They just look so big, and honestly, seeing that just completely ruins how I feel about myself for the entire rest of the day. It's like I can't focus on anything else. 

Which is really dangerous when you're working with high-voltage equipment, you know? I was working on this aluminum pontoon boat repair last week. Aluminum is so tricky because it doesn't change color before it melts. With steel, you get that nice cherry red, so you know exactly when you're about to blow a hole through it. But aluminum? It just looks shiny and then suddenly—bam—it just drops out and you've got a gaping hole to fill. 

And you have to clean it so thoroughly. You have to use a dedicated stainless steel wire brush. You can't use a brush that you've previously used on carbon steel, because you'll embed carbon particles into the aluminum, and it'll contaminate the weld. It'll get all porous and weak. I actually keep my aluminum brushes in a separate, sealed plastic container so Dave doesn't accidentally grab one to scrub off some rusty bumper. He does that, you know. He just grabs whatever tool is closest. It drives me absolutely crazy. 

But yeah, if I see my reflection and I look big, my whole day is just shot. I can't even enjoy a good, clean weld bead after that.
Has your concern about your weight or body shape ever interfered with your ability to focus or perform your job effectively?

Well, yeah, it actually has been causing some problems lately at the shop. The occupational health nurse flagged my weight a little while ago, and because of that, they've been keeping me off some of the heavy press work. They're pressuring me to go to urgent care and get all these checkups, which is totally messing up my shifts. I'm losing hours, and it's making it really hard to keep up with the bills at home. 

And speaking of the press work, we just got this new hydraulic press brake in. It's an absolute beast, like 150 tons of bending force. It's got this CNC backgauge that is supposed to be super precise, down to the thousandth of an inch. But the software interface is so clunky. It looks like it was programmed in the 90s. I was trying to set up a sequence for these complex brackets we were making for a local agricultural supply company, and the touchscreen kept freezing. 

I had to reboot the whole machine like three times. And when you reboot it, you have to re-home all the axes, which takes forever. Dave was getting so impatient, tapping his foot and huffing. But I told him, if we don't calibrate it right, the bend angles are going to be off, and then the brackets won't fit the tractor frames, and they'll reject the whole batch. You can't just eyeball a 90-degree bend on quarter-inch steel plate, you know? It has to be exact. But yeah, because they flagged my weight, I haven't even been allowed to operate it much, which is just really frustrating and stressful with the money situation.
Even though others have told you that you look thin or underweight, does the fear of gaining weight or becoming larger still feel just as intense to you?

I mean, yeah, people say that, but it doesn't change anything for me. The fear is still just... it's always there, screaming at me. Even if someone tells me I look thin, it's like my brain just doesn't believe them. I still feel terrified of getting bigger. 

Which is kind of like when people tell me a weld looks fine when it's clearly undercut. Like, Dave will look at a joint and say, "Ah, it's good enough, it'll hold." But I know it won't! Undercut is when you melt away the base metal along the toes of the weld, and you don't fill it back in with the filler rod. It creates this tiny little groove, and that groove is a stress riser. 

If that part is under any kind of dynamic load, like vibration or tension, that groove is exactly where the crack is going to start. I was trying to explain this to the new apprentice we got last month. He's this young kid, thinks he knows everything because he took a six-week course at the community college. He was running a MIG gun way too hot and moving too fast, leaving undercut everywhere. I told him he needed to turn his voltage down a hair and pause on the edges of his weave to let the puddle fill in. But he just rolled his eyes at me. 

It's so frustrating when you can clearly see a problem, and you know exactly how disastrous it's going to be, and someone else just completely dismisses it. You can't just ignore structural integrity, you know? It's like... it's going to fail eventually. But yeah, no matter what anyone says about my weight, the panic about gaining is just as intense as it always is.

You can't just eyeball a 90-degree bend on quarter-inch steel plate, you know? It has to be exact. But yeah, because they flagged my weight, I haven't even been allowed to operate it much, which is just really frustrating and stressful with the money situation.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's fear of weight gain or body shape concerns persist despite being underweight, which is critical in differentiating between anorexia nervosa and other eating disorders or conditions.
doctor.question: Even though others have told you that you look thin or underweight, does the fear of gaining weight or becoming larger still feel just as intense to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the intensity of the fear of gaining weight despite others saying the patient is thin. This aligns with the 'Fear of Weight Gain' symptom, but the patient has already discussed this symptom in a previous turn (Turn 7, where the doctor asked about the fear of gaining weight and the patient responded with 'if the scale goes up even a little bit, I just absolutely panic...'). The patient should not repeat the same symptom unless it's a completely different aspect, but here the doctor is just rephrasing the same fear of weight gain symptom. Therefore, I will return None as the symptom was already addressed.

patient.answer:
I mean, yeah, people say that, but it doesn't change anything for me. The fear is still just... it's always there, screaming at me. Even if someone tells me I look thin, it's like my brain just doesn't believe them. I still feel terrified of getting bigger. 

Which is kind of like when people tell me a weld looks fine when it's clearly undercut. Like, Dave will look at a joint and say, "Ah, it's good enough, it'll hold." But I know it won't! Undercut is when you melt away the base metal along the toes of the weld, and you don't fill it back in with the filler rod. It creates this tiny little groove, and that groove is a stress riser. 

If that part is under any kind of dynamic load, like vibration or tension, that groove is exactly where the crack is going to start. I was trying to explain this to the new apprentice we got last month. He's this young kid, thinks he knows everything because he took a six-week course at the community college. He was running a MIG gun way too hot and moving too fast, leaving undercut everywhere. I told him he needed to turn his voltage down a hair and pause on the edges of his weave to let the puddle fill in. But he just rolled his eyes at me. 

It's so frustrating when you can clearly see a problem, and you know exactly how disastrous it's going to be, and someone else just completely dismisses it. You can't just ignore structural integrity, you know? It's like... it's going to fail eventually. But yeah, no matter what anyone says about my weight, the panic about gaining is just as intense as it always is.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms align specifically with anorexia nervosa, restricting type, given the persistent restriction of food intake, intense fear of gaining weight, disturbance in self-perception of body weight/shape, and significant weight loss not better explained by another condition. No additional disorders from the previous list fit the clinical picture as closely.
